lesson.title: Personality Words and Making Adjectives Agree: -o / -a and Singular / Plural
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: Last week you met ser and its five forms — soy, eres, es, somos, son — and the four jobs it does: identity, origin, profession, and description. This week you push that fourth job as far as it goes: describing what a person is like on the inside, their personality. English lets you describe a boy and a girl with the very same word — 'a funny boy,' 'a funny girl.' Spanish makes the describing word change to match the person. That matching is called agreement, and by Friday it will feel automatic.

Here are seven words for personality. Each is shown in its base form — masculine and singular — which is how you would find it in a dictionary:

- [[trabajador]] — hardworking. Las abejas son muy trabajadoras.
- [[perezoso]] — lazy. A memory trick: the slow-moving animal English calls a 'sloth' is el perezoso in Spanish, named after this exact word.
- [[atrevido]] — daring, bold. An atrevido person is first in line for the tallest roller coaster and first to taste a food they have never tried.
- [[serio]] — serious. Not sad — just not joking around.
- [[gracioso]] — funny. A gracioso person makes the whole room laugh.
- [[ordenado]] — organized, neat. An ordenado person's backpack has a place for everything.
- [[desordenado]] — messy, disorganized. The exact opposite of ordenado.

A Spanish adjective changes to agree with — match — the person it describes, in two ways.

Gender. An adjective whose base form ends in -o switches to -a for a female:
- Mateo es serio. -> Ana es seria.
- Mi hermano es ordenado. -> Mi hermana es ordenada.
- perezoso -> perezosa, gracioso -> graciosa, atrevido -> atrevida, desordenado -> desordenada.

trabajador is the exception to watch. It ends in -or, not -o. As a rule, adjectives ending in a consonant look the same for males and females — but a small group ending in -or, including the personality word trabajador, do add -a: trabajador -> trabajadora. So Diego es trabajador, but Lucía es trabajadora. (The -or words that do not add -a are the ones meaning 'more' or 'less' of something, like mayor and menor — you will meet those later.)

Number. For more than one person, add -s after a vowel or -es after a consonant:
- serio -> serios / seria -> serias
- ordenada -> ordenadas
- trabajador -> trabajadores / trabajadora -> trabajadoras

An all-female group takes the -as form: Ana y Lucía son serias. An all-male or mixed group takes the -os form: Ana y Mateo son serios. That is the same 'a mixed group goes masculine' rule you saw with ellos last week.

Not every adjective ends in -o. Some end in -e (like inteligente, 'intelligent') and some end in a consonant (like gris, 'gray,' or popular). These do not change for gender at all — un amigo inteligente, una amiga inteligente, exactly the same word. But they still change for number:
- inteligente -> inteligentes
- gris -> grises (una tarde gris, unos días grises)
- popular -> populares

So with gris, the gender of what you are describing makes no difference — only how many.

You now have seven personality words and the two moves every Spanish adjective can make: gender (-o / -a, plus trabajador's special -a) and number (-s / -es). Tomorrow you will load them into a sentence frame built for comparison: 'Yo soy... pero mi amigo es...'.

config.instructions: Match each Spanish personality word to its English meaning.

objectives: Give the meaning of the seven personality adjectives introduced this week (trabajador, perezoso, atrevido, serio, gracioso, ordenado, desordenado)
Change an -o adjective to agree in gender (serio -> seria) and number (serio -> serios), and apply the -or -> -ora pattern to trabajador
Explain that adjectives ending in -e or a consonant (inteligente, gris) change for number but not for gender
materialsNeeded: Device for the matching activity (optional — can be done as a card-sort on paper)
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Recall last week's close: ser's fourth job is description — this week is all about personality.
2. Read the seven personality words aloud together, one example sentence each. Linger on el perezoso (the animal) as a memory hook.
3. Teach the gender rule with the Mateo/Ana pairs, then the number rule.
4. Slow down on trabajador — write 'trabajador -> trabajadora' on the board and contrast it with a plain consonant adjective. This is the week's trickiest form.
5. Teach the -e / consonant adjectives (inteligente, gris) as the 'gender does not matter, number still does' group.
6. Play the matching activity (adjective <-> meaning).
7. Complete the worksheet.
8. Preview tomorrow's 'Yo soy... pero mi amigo es...' frame.
differentiationTips: Struggling: work with just four -o adjectives (serio, gracioso, ordenado, perezoso) and only the gender rule today; add number and trabajador tomorrow
Ready for more: have them write the full grid for one adjective — masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural — then do the same for trabajador
If a child writes 'trabajadora' for a boy or 'serio' for a girl, point back to the person, not the word: 'Who are we describing? Is that a boy or a girl?'
teacherGuide.answerKey: Meanings: trabajador = hardworking, perezoso = lazy, atrevido = daring, serio = serious, gracioso = funny, ordenado = organized/neat, desordenado = messy. Gender: serio -> seria, ordenado -> ordenada, trabajador -> trabajadora. Number: gracioso -> graciosos, seria -> serias, trabajadora -> trabajadoras. inteligente and gris do not change for gender (inteligentes, grises for plural).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Opens week 5's WA-WL-2015.1.3 Presentational Communication target by front-loading the two things every later day depends on: the personality vocabulary itself and the adjective-agreement system (gender -o/-a, number -s/-es, and the trabajador -> trabajadora sub-pattern the scope-and-sequence names explicitly). Builds directly on week 4's ser, since every description this week is ser + an agreeing adjective.

generationData.instructions: Use today's personality words and the agreement rules (-o/-a for gender, -s/-es for number) to answer each question.

rows.problem: Write the feminine singular form of each adjective: serio -> ___, ordenado -> ___, trabajador -> ___.
Fill in the blank: Mi hermana es muy ___ (hardworking). Mi hermano es muy ___ (hardworking).
Make it plural: 'Ana y Lucía son ___ (gracioso).' 'Mateo y Ana son ___ (serio).'
The adjective 'inteligente' ends in -e. Does it change for a girl vs. a boy? Does it change for one person vs. two? Explain.
